O.outcome_detail: distribution of item complexity across the combined item bank

cells.quote: "Across all assessments, 38 items (38%) assessed a single LO and another 39 items (39%) assessed two LOs. Twenty items (20%) assessed three LOs, while only four items assessed four or more LOs."
cells.note: This sentence appears in the wiki entry rather than the supplied study-text excerpt; the finding is descriptive and reports no superiority contrast.

O.outcome_detail: coverage and concentration of the 14 learning objectives

cells.quote: The FCI [1] is a 30-item multiple-choice assessment that probes students’ conceptual understanding of force and motion, contrasting Newtonian reasoning with common informal beliefs about mechanics. Physics instructors use it more widely than any other mechanics RBA [4]. The FMCE [2] covers content similar to the FCI, kinematics and Newton’s laws, in 47 multiple-choice items. Several items share a physical scenario and ask students to select the response consistent with their reasoning about that scenario. The FMCE includes a small number of items on energy. The EMCS [3] is a 25-item multiple-choice assessment focused on energy and momentum, covering concepts such as kinetic and potential energy, work, and conservation principles that the FCI and FMCE do not address. Together, these three assessments cover the core topics of introductory mechanics.
cells.note: The entry additionally reports that the three RBAs cover all 14 LOs with at least six items per LO; that exact coverage result is not stated in the supplied study text excerpt.

O.outcome_detail: continued use of research-based instructional strategies

cells.quote: The fraction of this sample of UBC faculty who used RBIS and then quit is 1 out of 70, or less than 1/20th of what Henderson, Dancy, and Niewiadomska-Bugaj found1.
cells.note: Observational comparison of CWSEI-supported UBC faculty with the prior survey of physics faculty; faculty were not randomly assigned.

O.outcome_detail: fidelity of implementation

cells.quote: With three caveats, the fidelity appears to be maintained quite well; with little change from when faculty were using RBIS with the help of the SESs.
cells.note: The study reports an informal, incomplete SES assessment rather than a statistical comparison; ns is used because no power or equivalence test is reported.

D.treatment: Prior CWSEI-supported RBIS adoption with opportunity to teach another course
D.comparison: Opportunity without subsequent RBIS use in another course

O.outcome_detail: adoption of RBIS in additional courses

cells.quote: Twenty-three of the 25 RBIS users on the PHAS faculty were found to be using RBIS in additional courses. Four of the 29 non-quitting EOAS faculty have not taught a different undergraduate course. Of the remaining 25, 23 have implemented RBIS in additional courses.
cells.note: This is a descriptive follow-up among faculty who had adopted RBIS with CWSEI support; the comparison is between those who did and did not subsequently use RBIS in another course, not a randomized treatment comparison.

D.comparison: earlier period before or during less CWSEI involvement

O.outcome_detail: faculty belief in research-based instructional strategies

cells.quote: There were some other faculty members in every department who did not believe in RBIS and simply refused to use them. The fraction of the faculty with those beliefs has noticeably decreased over time in every department that has a CWSEI supported initiative. In EOAS, where there has been the most widespread involvement, with about ¾ of the faculty having worked with an SES, it is now nearly zero, and in PHAS it has dropped markedly with time, although it still remains a significant fraction.
cells.note: The authors describe this as an impression based on their work with faculty; the text states that they do not have data on the fraction in some other departments.

D.comparison: faculty-desired assessments measuring skills, perceptions, and specific concepts

O.outcome_detail: perceived breadth and applicability of assessment measures

result.effect: 23 of 24 participants discussed the Limited Measure family

cells.quote: Faculty think that RBAs are limited and don’t measure many of the things they care about, or aren’t applicable in their classes. Instead they want assessments to measure skills, perceptions and specific concepts.

D.treatment: professional monitors learning through onsite apprenticeship and experience
D.comparison: volunteers learning through a PowerPoint lecture

O.outcome_detail: ability to make nuanced qualitative stream assessments

cells.quote: Professionals learned to make assessments in an apprenticeship under more experienced monitors, whereas volunteers learned about the measures through a PowerPoint lecture that outlined the protocol measures, but did not transfer any nuanced or practical assessment skills.
cells.note: The study reports an observed contrast, not a controlled intervention.

O.outcome_detail: ability to compare streams and make qualitative assessments

cells.quote: Notably, the biggest difference between professionals and volunteers was the number of streams each group had experience evaluating; professionals visited many more streams than volunteers, and were thus able to more easily compare them.
cells.note: The direction is based on the study's qualitative comparison of professionals and volunteers.

D.treatment: personal evaluations followed by discussion and group agreement
D.comparison: individual interpretation of written protocol scales

O.outcome_detail: qualitative RBP assessment

cells.quote: Monitors first made personal evaluations, then compared their evaluations with a partner or group members, and settled on a numeric assessment for the metric.
cells.note: The comparison is supported by the study's description of volunteer PowerPoint training, which did not transfer nuanced or practical assessment skills.

D.treatment: professional contextual knowledge and personal experience
D.comparison: literal interpretation of the written RBP scale

O.outcome_detail: interpretation of embeddedness and channelization categories

cells.quote: For instance, during a professional training session, monitors explained that a scale measuring embeddedness of particles in a stream bed (RBP protocol 2a [Barbour et al. 1999]) should not be interpreted linearly, even though it was written to suggest linearity: the written scale suggests that 25% is suboptimal quality and 75% is poor quality. Professional monitors explained that realistically, more than 25% embeddedness should be characterized as poor quality because the environment becomes unsuitable for macroinvertebrates.
cells.note: The study also reports that the protocol's subjectivity and imprecision compelled reliance on background knowledge and personal experience; this is a qualitative interpretation contrast, not a measured accuracy effect.

D.treatment: RBL integrated with STEM and IoT/hypermedia learning activities

O.outcome_detail: students' metaliteracy in solving a tessellation decoration problem

cells.quote: Metalliteration cannot be realized with the traditional classroom system, the use of the Intern et of Things (IoT) and hypermedia in learning with a specific approach is one strategy to achieve metalliteracy.
cells.note: The study presents a proposed RBL-STEM learning framework and reports no empirical comparison or outcome data; therefore the direction is not established.

cells.quote: In 2008, about ⅓ (23%/72% = 32%) of those who tried ended up discontinuing useof all RBISs. In 2019, discontinuation is a very low 5% of those who tried a RBIS.
cells.note: The contrast compares independent survey cohorts rather than randomly assigned conditions; the printed percentages are descriptive.
